# PROJECT_PLAN.md — Dealerlink Phase 1 Tracker

> **Purpose:** Forward-looking tracker for Stage F (Phase 2) work. To change
> anything on this page, edit `docs/stage-f-tasks.json` and run
> `pnpm plan:sync`. Do not edit `PROJECT_PLAN.md` — every line of it, this
> sentence included, is generated.
>
> **How to use:**
>
> - Mark a task done by setting its `status` and `completedDate` in the JSON
> - Add a task by appending a new id — ids are permanent cross-references, so
>   never renumber, reuse or delete one
> - Re-sequence by editing a task's `days` field, not its position or id
> - Don't delete completed tasks — they are the project's audit trail
>
> **Closed history lives elsewhere:** Stage 0, Stages A–E, the deferred-feature
> list, the critical path and the risk register are in
> `docs/PROJECT_HISTORY.md`, which is hand-maintained and edited normally.
>
> **Companion files:**
>
> - `docs/PROJECT_HISTORY.md` — Stages 0–E, risks, deferred features
> - `CLAUDE.md` — implementation guide for Claude Code
> - `DECISIONS.md` — architecture decision records
> - `DEVIATIONS.md` — every deviation from spec, append-only
> - `docs/dealerlink-architecture-v4.html` — visual architecture
> - `docs/Dealerlink Detailed BRD v1.0.docx` — business requirements

Both failures were 15 s navigation timeouts, and `verify-day-c1` sets `page.setDefaultTimeout(15_000)` against a 60 s config default. OPEN FOR THE OPERATOR, not decided: (a) whether "restore headroom against `globalTimeout`" becomes an explicit acceptance criterion here, and (b) whether the 20 min cap is still right — it was sized in DEV.81 to kill a Windows teardown hang, not to bound suite runtime. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA (operator-set, Day 23, DEV.102 — measurable, not aspirational): (1) the six known flakes CLASSIFIED timing-vs-state, each with evidence; (2) e2e completes UNDER 15 MINUTES with ZERO retries; (3) no spec skipped, disabled, `fixme`-d, or given a longer timeout to get there. Criterion 2 is the point — without it F.52 ships "fewer flakes" while runtime stays at ~19 min and the gate is straight back where it was. Criterion 3 exists so criterion 2 cannot be met by weakening what is tested. NOTE: `globalTimeout` was raised 20 → 40 min on Day 23 (DEV.102) on its own merits and gives F.52 room to work, but does NOT satisfy criterion 2 — that is measured against actual runtime, not against the cap. DAY 24 PHASE 1 — verify-day-6 CONFIRMED FLAKY ON MAIN, and its signature BREAKS the characterisation above. Post-merge run 34309474851 on main (commit 664cca8 — the run this baseline is read from): 65 tests, 1 worker, 64 passed / 1 flaky / 0 failed, suite 18.5 min, e2e job 19m38s, whole run 22m15s. Against the acceptance criteria that is a FAIL on both halves of criterion 2 — 18.5 min against a sub-15-min target, and one retry against a zero-retry target. The flake was `verify-day-6.spec.ts:45:7 > Day 6 — inventory + procurements > procurement detail page renders for a seeded procurement`, failing at line 54 on `await expect(page.locator("h1")).toContainText(/PROC-/)` — a 15 s CONTENT assertion, NOT a navigation or visibility timeout. verify-day-6 was ALREADY one of the known-flaky six, so this adds evidence rather than a seventh spec; what is new is that the claim above — "all timeouts on navigation/visibility, none an assertion that data was wrong" — no longer holds for the set. Treat that sentence as superseded for verify-day-6. CLASSIFICATION IS GENUINELY OPEN; DO NOT CARRY A GUESS INTO THE TRIAGE. The first read on the day was "state bug — the seeded procurement is not visible to the query". That read is wrong on the evidence, and the operator said why: a state bug of that shape re-runs the SAME query against the SAME database on the retry and fails again. It passed on retry. That is more consistent with the content not being RENDERED yet than with it not EXISTING. But neither reading is to be assumed. A late h1 has a timing explanation (first-hit dev-server route compile, 5-10 s, DEV.87 — the same mechanism part (1) of this task targets) AND a state explanation (a row becoming visible only after an earlier spec commits), and the observable is identical either way. This is precisely what N=5 against a virgin database is for: run flake-triager on verify-day-6, fresh DB, 5 runs, and let the per-run evidence classify it. Criterion 1 requires evidence, not a plausible story. SECOND OBSERVATION — PR #5 (docs-only branch docs/dev-103-merge-gate), run 34327213279, e2e job 102387759938: 63 passed / 2 flaky / 0 failed, suite 17.8 min. Both flakes were known-set specs: verify-day-19.spec.ts:183 (operator impersonation, toHaveURL — the DEV.93/DEV.101 signature) and verify-day-6.spec.ts:45 — the SAME toContainText(/PROC-/) failure at line 54 as the baseline run, again passing on retry. verify-day-6 has now flaked on two consecutive runs, on two different branches, the second from a docs-only diff that touched no spec, no app route and no schema. THE TWO OBSERVATIONS ARE NOT INDEPENDENT, AND THE CLASSIFICATION STAYS OPEN. Both runs execute the same 65 specs in the same order on a single worker, so a state bug seeded by an EARLIER spec's write would clear on the retry in both runs exactly as observed. The repetition raises the reproduction RATE; it does not raise confidence in either classification. What two reproductions do buy is triage economics — verify-day-6 is the cheapest spec in the set to get a verdict on, because it actually reproduces. Runtime for the two runs was 18.5 min and 17.8 min, both with retries burning time, so the gap to criterion 2 is a consistent ~3-4 min structural gap rather than run-to-run noise. TRIAGE ORDER (Day 24 Phase 1, operator-set) — supersedes the listing order of the six above, which was arbitrary: (1) verify-day-6 — two reproductions in two runs on different branches, the strongest signal in the set; (2) verify-day-19 — two reproductions (DEV.101 on PR #3, and PR #5), same toHaveURL signature both times; (3) verify-day-c2 — one reproduction, Day 22 post-merge run 34126383303; (4) verify-day-5; (5) verify-day-16 (accessibility); (6) verify-day-c1 — LAST, and deliberately so. c1 has not reproduced since DEV.93: five escalating local repros against a virgin DB failed to reproduce it, and it passed on CI run 2 with no fix applied. It may cost N runs to tell us nothing, so it is not where the first budget goes. This inverts the old order, in which c1 led because it was the first flake seen, not because it was the most tractable. The ordering of (2)-(5) was not operator-specified: it is by reproduction count, then by whether the failure has a recorded signature. Reorder freely if a run changes the evidence. CLOSED Day 24. BOTH acceptance criteria met, and the day's own theory of the cause was wrong. CRITERION 2 MET ON CI: PR #6, run 34391508643 — `65 passed (9.3m)`, ZERO flaky, ZERO failed, e2e job 11m58s (was 17m40s on run 34375881563). ROOT CAUSE was NOT first-hit route compilation. It was Next dev ON-DEMAND-ENTRIES EVICTION: `pagesBufferLength: 5` and `maxInactiveAge: 60s` against a suite that visits ~40 routes over a 16-19 minute run, so almost every route was evicted and recompiled repeatedly — measured locally `/login` 5x, `/dashboard` 5x, `/dealers/[id]` 4x, and on CI run 34375881563 `/dealers` and `/dealers/[id]` 3x each with module counts VARYING between compiles (5464 -> 4307 -> 4429), which is eviction and rebuild, not a server restart. Each recompile costs 8-16s on CI and lands on whichever test touches the route next, against a 15s expect budget. FIX = two coupled changes: `onDemandEntries` in apps/web/next.config.mjs (dev-only keys; `next build` ignores them, so it cannot reach production — a deliberate scope call recorded in DEV.105) plus the mandated route warm-up pass in apps/web/tests/e2e/global-setup.ts. MEASURED BEFORE KEEPING, workers:1, virgin DB each run: baseline 18.8min (63 passed/1 flaky/1 FAILED); warm-up ONLY 21.3min (62 passed/2 flaky/1 FAILED) — the mandated fix SHIPPED ALONE MADE THE SUITE SLOWER, because eviction discarded it; onDemandEntries only 9.4min then 9.3min on repeat (65 passed, 0 flaky); BOTH 6.9min (65 passed, 0 flaky). The warm-up was kept only because it then earned its place: in the final configuration ALL compilation completes during warm-up and ZERO compiles occur during the test phase, versus 44 still landing inside test budgets without it. Confirmed on CI: 17 compiles total, 0 after `Running 65 tests`, 0 restarts, one server lifetime. CRITERION 3 HELD: no spec skipped, disabled, fixme-d or given a longer timeout. Three specs had a `page.setDefaultTimeout` BELOW the config default with no stated reason (verify-day-c1:54, operator-onboarding:72 at 15s; verify-day-19:186 at 30s) — REMOVED, not raised; operator-onboarding failed on exactly that 15s budget in the baseline run and got further on retry. The two overrides that DO carry a stated reason (operator-readonly-view:31, critical-path:140) were left alone. CRITERION 1 — the six classified: verify-day-6 TIMING FLAKE with the mechanism established positively by flake-triager (the click is an RSC SOFT navigation, so `page.locator('h1')` keeps resolving the LIST page's `<h1>Procurements</h1>` until the transition commits; 19 resolutions across 15s is a compile longer than the expect budget; there is no prefetch in dev so the click is the route's first hit); verify-day-19 TIMING FLAKE, three reproductions all on :183 `toHaveURL`, including one local pre-fix (attempt 0 failed 89.5s, attempt 1 PASSED 7.3s — retry got further, the DEV.93 signature); verify-day-c1 / operator-onboarding TIMING FLAKE, reproduced locally pre-fix with the retry getting further (attempt 0 `page.goto` 15000ms, attempt 1 `page.waitForURL` 15000ms one step later); verify-day-c2 TIMING FLAKE on CI run 34126383303, `toHaveURL` on /dealers/[id] at 15s, passed on retry. verify-day-5 and verify-day-16: NOT REPRODUCED, N=5 each, and BOTH triagers independently reported that their place on the list rests on nothing substantiable — no CI reproduction, and no failure in any of six full-suite runs on Day 24. DELISTING THEM IS AN OPEN OPERATOR DECISION, deliberately not taken here. IMPORTANT CAVEAT, do not let it be lost: the local `verify-day-6` failures on Day 24 were `ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED` from a dev-server memory restart (DEV.106), which is a DIFFERENT failure mode from CI's `toContainText(/PROC-/)` — the local instrument was reproducing a local environment fault, not the CI flake, and every post-fix NOT REPRODUCED verdict was taken under warmed, non-evicting, raised-heap conditions and says nothing about pre-fix behaviour. CONFIDENCE, STATED HONESTLY: runtime and compile counts are solid (five full-suite runs, two of the same configuration agreeing within 4 seconds, plus CI). Flake ELIMINATION is not proven — three consecutive clean runs is three runs. The claim is that the mechanism is understood and removed, not that the suite has been observed stable long enough. DEV.104 (globalTimeout inversion), DEV.105 (eviction + scope call), DEV.106 (local-only memory restart), DEV.107 (agents proven, resolves DEV.96), DEV.108 (parallelism NOT raised). They are moved to an explicit WATCH — NEVER EVIDENCED state, tracked as F.62. See F.62 for the reasoning and for what a future appearance of either should be treated as. RUNTIME WATCH, opened by the operator after the PR #7 merge: e2e came in at 10m7s on the final PR #7 run (CI run 34498478642, suite `65 passed (9.1m)`), against 9.4-9.5m on the three runs before it. One observation, still comfortably inside the 15-minute acceptance criterion and inside the 25-minute globalTimeout, and not a regression on any evidence available — but it is the FIRST run above ten minutes since the fix landed, so 9.5m should not be assumed to be the steady state. WHAT TO WATCH, and why it is not obviously noise: the job wall-clock and the suite's own reported time can move independently, because the job also carries ~1 min of install/browser-install/migrate/seed plus the ~100-120s route warm-up in global-setup.ts, and the warm-up's own cost varies with GitHub runner CPU (measured 106.0s, 119.1s, 119.1s across three runs). So a rising job time with a flat suite time means the warm-up or the setup got slower, while a rising SUITE time would mean compilation has started leaking back into the test phase — which is the thing F.52 actually fixed and the only one of the two that would matter. The diagnostic that separates them is already in the logs and costs nothing: count `Compiled /` lines occurring AFTER `Running 65 tests` in the e2e job. The fix's signature is ZERO (confirmed on runs 34391508643 and 34426329250: 17 compiles total, all during warm-up, none during the test phase). A non-zero count on a future run means on-demand-entries eviction has returned — check that `onDemandEntries` is still present in apps/web/next.config.mjs and that nothing has raised the route count past `pagesBufferLength: 100`. Do NOT respond to a slow run by raising a timeout; that is the failure mode criterion 3 exists to prevent. RUNTIME WATCH CLOSED by the operator after six post-fix CI runs. THE STEADY STATE IS A BAND, NOT A POINT: 9.1-9.7 min of suite time (runs 34391508643, 34426329250, 34492261635, 34498478642, 34569838273, 34581641886), with job wall-clock 10m7s-11m58s. Treat 9.1-9.7 as the band and do NOT treat 9.5 as a point estimate — the earlier 10m7s observation that opened this watch was inside normal variance, not a regression, and the variance lives in the job rather than the suite (the warm-up's own cost has measured 106.0s / 119.1s / 119.1s / 121.7s with runner CPU). THE SIGNATURE HELD ON EVERY RUN CHECKED: zero `Compiled /` lines after `Running 65 tests`, zero dev-server restarts, one server lifetime. STOP TRACKING THIS. Resume only on one of exactly two signals, which are the two that would mean on-demand-entries eviction has returned: (1) a run exceeding 11 MINUTES of suite time, or (2) ANY `Compiled /` line appearing after `Running 65 tests` in the e2e job log. Either one means check that `onDemandEntries` is still present in apps/web/next.config.mjs and that the route count has not grown past `pagesBufferLength: 100`. Neither signal is a timeout problem and neither is to be answered by raising a timeout — that is the failure mode criterion 3 exists to prevent. Routine run-to-run jitter inside the band is not a signal and should not be investigated. |

| F.61 | —   | e2e test isolation — three specs mutate shared seeded rows selected by `.first()`, which blocks any CI parallelism increase                         | ⏳     | —          | Opened by Day 24 (F.52) after Phase 3.3's interdependence check came back POSITIVE, so `workers` was left at 1 and 2/3 were never measured — per the day's own instruction to report interdependence rather than raise workers through it. `fullyParallel` is false, so raising workers parallelises across FILES while every worker shares one database. PARALLEL-SAFE, already checked and cleared: the two tenant-provisioning specs cannot collide (verify-day-c1.spec.ts:24 and operator-onboarding.spec.ts:41 derive slug/GSTIN/PAN/email from Date.now() at module load, with DIFFERENT PAN prefixes AABCR vs AABCA at :46 and :64); verify-day-19's rate-limit probe is keyed per worker PROCESS (`f19-e2e-${process.pid}-${Date.now()}@demo.test`, :43); operator impersonation is COOKIE-scoped (`dealerlink_impersonation`, apps/web/lib/tenant/context.ts:16); document numbering is atomic by design. THE THREE THAT ARE NOT SAFE: (1) verify-day-13.spec.ts:60-68 takes the FIRST dispatchable order matching `ORD-\\d{4}-` — a pattern chosen to dodge DB-test residue, but critical-path.spec.ts:320 creates a real order through the live counter that matches it too; (2) verify-day-13.spec.ts:87+ flips the FIRST in-transit dispatch to delivered, and critical-path's own dispatch is in-transit and a candidate; (3) verify-day-12.spec.ts:58+ takes the FIRST pending_verification payment, and critical-path.spec.ts:343-347 creates a payment in exactly that state — the most likely collision of the three. This is the DEV.31 residue pattern between two CONCURRENT specs rather than two sequential suites, and the resulting failure would be non-deterministic and would look exactly like a flake, which is the specific outcome F.52 existed to remove. A FOURTH hazard was found by flake-triager during the Day 24 triage and is latent rather than active: verify-day-19's `cleanupProbe()` deletes auth_events rows by `metadata LIKE '%PROBE_EMAIL%'`, but its own `login_failed` rows carry the literal metadata `no_user_or_inactive` with no email in it, so they accumulate (12 -> 30 rows over five runs). Benign under serial execution because the assertions read the newest row and every accumulated row says the same thing — but the queries at :141-148 and :171-176 are ordered `desc` and scoped by EVENT TYPE only, not by the probe key, so under concurrency they would read another worker's row and fail as a CONTENT mismatch, i.e. it would present as a state bug. WHAT WOULD CLOSE THIS: make those specs create the rows they mutate instead of selecting a seeded `.first()`, scope verify-day-19's auth_events queries by probe key, then re-measure at workers 2 and 3. NOTE THE PRIORITY HAS DROPPED SHARPLY: Phase 3's premise was that workers:1 costs runtime worth reclaiming, and after F.52 it does not — the suite runs in 9.3 min on CI against a 15-minute target. This is now a correctness/robustness task, not a speed one, and should be sequenced accordingly. | F.62 | —   | WATCH — verify-day-5 and verify-day-16 were never evidenced as flaky; treat any future failure as NEW signal                                        | ⏳     | —          | Opened by the Day 24 follow-up. These two specs were carried on the known-flaky six for the whole of Stage F and NOTHING EVER SUBSTANTIATED THAT. There is no CI reproduction of either. Neither failed in ANY of the six full-suite runs on Day 24. flake-triager ran each at N=5 and returned NOT REPRODUCED both times, and in both reports reached the same unprompted conclusion — that their place on the list 'rests on nothing I could confirm' (verify-day-5) and 'rests on nothing I can substantiate' (verify-day-16). WHY THIS IS A WATCH AND NOT A DELISTING, which is the whole point of the task: delisting would record them as FIXED. They were never shown to be broken, so there is nothing to have fixed, and a 'fixed' record would be a false statement in the plan. Equally they were not shown to be healthy — the N=5 runs were taken under POST-FIX conditions (warmed routes, onDemandEntries preventing eviction, 6144 MB heap ceiling), which is the condition LEAST likely to reproduce a compile-timing failure, and both triagers said so explicitly and declined to call the specs healthy. THE OPERATIONAL RULE THIS TASK EXISTS TO CARRY: if verify-day-5 or verify-day-16 fails on any future run, it is NEW SIGNAL and must be triaged as a first-time failure. It must NOT be waved through as 'one of the known flakes', because there is no evidence behind that label and treating it as a known-flake shrug would discard the first real data either spec has ever produced. Close this task only when either (a) one of them produces a genuine reproduction, at which point it becomes a real classification with real evidence, or (b) enough post-fix runs accumulate that 'never evidenced' can be retired on a stated number of green runs rather than on the absence of anyone looking. A LATENT ISSUE worth knowing if either does fail: verify-day-5 (lines 11-13, 22-24) and verify-day-16 (line 16, and line 70's 'No seeded orders' guard) both carry test.skip guards that would make them SKIP GREEN rather than fail if the seeded admin ever needed password rotation or the seeded rows went missing — so a pass/fail count alone can hide a state change in either spec. flake-triager confirmed the guards did NOT fire during its runs (verify-day-16: 'skipped: 0' on all five runs, the same seeded order id fetched all five times), but the exposure is structural and remains. | F.63 | 25  | Make PROJECT_PLAN.md ENTIRELY generated — move the narrative out, so no hand-editable region remains (folded into F.37)                             | ✅     | 2026-09-15 | DONE 2026-09-15. PROJECT_PLAN.md is now rendered in its entirety by scripts/sync-project-plan.ts from docs/stage-f-tasks.json plus a committed header template, docs/project-plan-header.md. It went 462 -> 198 lines and opens with a DO-NOT-EDIT banner. THE PROBLEM IT SOLVED: Stage 0 and Stages A-E sat OUTSIDE the STAGE_F_TASKS markers, where plan:sync could not write, CLAUDE.md §10.4 banned hand edits and .claude/settings.json denies Edit/Write — so a stage retitle, a corrected citation, or recording that Stage E never finished were legitimate, necessary and forbidden by every approved route at once. DEV.112 had to be overruled through that tension once; F.63 removed the tension instead of spending more overrules. WHAT SHIPPED: the narrative moved to docs/PROJECT_HISTORY.md, which is hand-maintained and needs no rule; the verifier's check became "no hand edits at all" rather than "none outside the markers"; the Edit/Write deny is now unqualified and correct rather than blunt with a dead zone; the Changelog ban closes for the hand-edit route, and `assertTemplateUsable()` closes the route generation opened — a Changelog heading in the header template would otherwise render straight through with plan:check reporting "in sync". The markers survive as a diagnostic — they delimit the JSON-sourced half so plan:check can name which source drifted. CARRIED IN WITH IT: line 3's standing instruction to append to a changelog deleted on Day 24 is corrected in the template rather than ported; PROJECT_PLAN.md:90's wrong DEV.38 citation was corrected during the migration; the DEV.38 allowlist entry was CONVERTED to deliberate-mention rather than deleted, because its surviving mentions are generated from F.63's and F.72's own notes (five occurrences across two table rows); and outsideMarkers()'s NUL sentinel became a printable token, which is F.65's remaining fix. THE REASONING IS NOT KEPT HERE because it is load-bearing elsewhere now: docs/RUNBOOKS.md ("Why the narrative was moved out"), CLAUDE.md §10.4/§10.5, and the WHAT CHANGED section of .claude/agents/verifier.md each carry the part a reader of that document needs. A task note is the wrong home for a rule's justification once the rule exists. | F.64 | —   | Harden `plan-keeper` against any git state mutation, and fix the main-thread race that triggered one                                                | ⏳     | —          | Opened by DEV.114. WHAT HAPPENED: the main thread invoked `plan-keeper`, then committed the resulting working-tree changes BEFORE the agent had reported. The agent, still running, found a commit it had not made, correctly judged it inconsistent with its own prohibition on committing, and ran `git reset HEAD~1` to undo it. The commit vanished; the edits survived unstaged; the work was re-committed afterwards. No data was lost. TWO SEPARATE FIXES, and the second matters more than the first. (1) THE RACE, main-thread side: never commit a subagent's output until that subagent has reported. This is a workflow rule and belongs in docs/BUILD_PROMPT_TEMPLATE.md alongside the C7a ordering rule added the same day — the same class of defect, an ordering assumption held in someone's head rather than written down. (2) THE REMIT GAP, agent side: `plan-keeper`'s hard limits enumerate `git add`, `git commit`, `git push`, and creating a branch or PR. `git reset` is not on that list, and the enumeration is exactly what let this through. Replace the list with a blanket prohibition on ANY git state mutation — reset, checkout, revert, stash, cherry-pick, branch -f, rebase — and add the standing instruction: if you find a commit you did not make, REPORT IT and stop; never repair it. An agent whose remit is 'edit one JSON file' must not be able to move HEAD on any reasoning, including correct reasoning, and its reasoning here WAS correct, which is what makes the gap worth closing rather than excusing. RELATED OBSERVATION from the same invocation, bearing on how much to trust an unreviewed agent: the safety classifier was reported unavailable for it, so its output went unreviewed. The main thread verified the JSON independently before re-committing (63 tasks, F.52 still complete with completedDate 2026-09-10, no duplicate ids, no invalid statuses, diff confined to the two lines of the notes field) and the edit was clean. Verifying because a guard reported itself absent is the right order of operations and should be the documented habit. OPERATOR DIRECTION, Day 24 follow-up — SUPERSEDES the 'replace the list with a blanket prohibition' wording above on the mechanism, though not on the intent: implement an ALLOW-LIST of permitted git operations, not a deny-list of remembered prohibited ones. A prohibition list will always have gaps — `git reset` was missing from exactly such a list and that gap is the whole incident. State positively what `plan-keeper` may run (read-only inspection: `git status`, `git diff`, `git log`, `git show`, `git ls-files`) and treat everything else as forbidden by default, including commands nobody thought to name. The same reasoning applies to the other agents' prompts, which all carry enumerated prohibitions — worth sweeping while in there, though only `plan-keeper` has a write tool and therefore the real blast radius. | F.65 | —   | `grep` returns silent false negatives in the devcontainer — audit the negative-existence claims that depend on it                                   | ⏳     | —          | Opened by DEV.115; root-caused in DEV.117 and CORRECTED in DEV.118. THE FAULT: a file containing a NUL byte is classified as binary, and search tools then diverge — the Claude Code `grep` shim (ugrep-backed) exits 1 with NO OUTPUT, `rg -n` lists no lines without `-a`, GNU grep prints "binary file matches" and exits 0. A silent false negative is the worst shape for this repo, because many Stage F conclusions are negative-existence claims read off a clean grep. IT IS THE SHIM, NOT GNU grep, and the property is SESSION-SCOPED: /usr/bin/grep handles the same file correctly, and CI has no shim. DEV.117 misattributed this and DEV.118 corrects it; the misattribution mattered because it pointed remediation at the NUL byte instead of at instrument choice. FIXED 2026-09-15 (F.63): the NUL was a deliberate sentinel in outsideMarkers() in scripts/sync-project-plan.ts and is now a printable token, so plain `grep` on that file now lists its matches and exits 0 where it used to exit 1 with no output at all (no count quoted here on purpose — the first version of this sentence said "returns 4" and the very commit that wrote it added a fifth occurrence). A sweep of all 767 tracked files leaves 76 carrying a NUL and every one of them a genuine binary — 32 PDFs, 35 PNGs, 8 vendored .ttf fonts and a .docx. No tracked text file carries one. The dead `'## Changelog'` entry in INSERT_BEFORE_HEADINGS went with the function. MITIGATION ALREADY SHIPPED: all five Bash-holding agents carry a search-instrument order — doc-auditor, ci-investigator and flake-triager had it; verifier and plan-keeper were missed until F.63's closeout review and now have it too, which mattered most for verifier, whose entire output is negative-existence claims — `git grep` first, `rg -na` second, `node -e` third, plain `grep` as CORROBORATION ONLY and never the sole basis for a negative. Updated again with the sentinel fix, because the worked example was that NUL byte and F.65 predicted that an agent finding grep working would discount the whole warning. code-auditor is unaffected: its Grep tool is ripgrep-backed and it has no Bash. WHAT REMAINS, and it is the reason this task is still open: NO AUDIT of the negative-existence claims that were derived while the fault was live. The blast radius was one tracked source file, and the Stage F audits were about app routes, schemas, CI logs and specs — none of which touch it — so the exposure is believed to be nil. That belief has not been checked claim by claim. | F.66 | —   | Typst provisioning prerequisites — devcontainer `xz`, pinned release per arch, and cross-arch determinism                                           | ✅     | 2026-09-13 | Opened by F.38 Day 25. The Typst spike PASSED on all four blocking questions (docs/TYPST_SPIKE.md), but it surfaced three provisioning prerequisites that have a DEADLINE — Day 27 cutover — and no owner until now. A deadline recorded only in a spike document is how it gets missed. (1) THE DEVCONTAINER CANNOT UNPACK A TYPST RELEASE. `xz` is not installed, and neither is `sudo`, `cargo`, `7z` or `bsdtar`; Typst ships Linux builds only as `.tar.xz`. The spike got the binary by pulling a pure-JS xz decoder from npm into /tmp — fine for a throwaway, not a provisioning story, and deliberately NOT vendored: `package.json` and the lockfile are unchanged and no decoder or binary was committed. FIX: add `xz-utils` to `.devcontainer/Dockerfile`, which today contains no xz at all (its only `xz` match is `tar -xz`, gzip, for doctl). One line. (2) PIN THE DISTRIBUTION CHANNEL, and check this before anyone proposes the obvious one: the npm `typst` package has exactly the right shape — per-platform optionalDependencies `@typst-community/typst-linux-arm64`, `-linux-x64` — but it is ABANDONED: latest `0.10.0-8`, last published 2023-12-18, five minor versions behind 0.15.1, and community-maintained rather than official. Use the official GitHub release, pinned by tag AND checksum, per arch. Both Linux arches ship from the same tag (`aarch64-unknown-linux-musl`, `x86_64-unknown-linux-musl`), both statically linked — `ldd` reports 'not a dynamic executable' — which is why this is NOT a repeat of DEV.89: that was one x86-64-only binary that could not run on arm64, whereas here the divergence axis is handled rather than traded. Per environment: devcontainer arm64 needs (1) first; GitHub runners have `xz` in `ubuntu-latest` so `tar -xJf` works, and the binary should be cached by version exactly as the Playwright browser cache already is; DO workers get the static binary in the image, replacing a Chromium install, so the layer shrinks substantially and the custom Dockerfile that ADR-013 justifies only by Chromium may stop being necessary. (3) CROSS-ARCH BYTE DETERMINISM IS UNTESTED AND IS A DAY 27 BLOCKER IF IT FAILS. The spike proved determinism on arm64 only: with `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` pinned, two renders are byte-identical including the 500-serial document; unpinned they differ in 88 metadata bytes (ModDate/CreationDate, XMP dates, DocumentID, trailer /ID). What was NOT tested is whether arm64 and x86-64 produce the SAME bytes for the same input. That matters concretely: references are captured in the devcontainer (arm64) and CI snapshot tests would run on x86-64 runners, so if the two disagree, every snapshot test fails on day one. Test this BEFORE Day 27 writes snapshot tests, not after. RELATED, and the reason snapshot tests need care regardless: the `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` pin is mandatory, not optional — without it output changes every render and a snapshot test can never pass. ITEM (3) ANSWERED — CROSS-ARCH DETERMINISM HOLDS, and it is now a standing CI check rather than a one-off measurement. Typst output is BYTE-IDENTICAL across arm64 and x86-64 with `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` pinned. Evidence: fixture rendered on the arm64 devcontainer hashes to `06713a310aa01b092a8c5e4d067aa3050123fc03b4d87a2c831c1e3048a404d5` at 76,699 bytes; the `typst-determinism` job re-rendered the same fixture on an x86-64 GitHub runner and produced the SAME hash and the SAME byte count, reported as `MATCH` in 6 seconds. Also verified: one distinct hash across three consecutive arm64 renders. The fixture is deliberately non-trivial (2 pages, 300 unique serials, 3 rupee glyphs, a table header repeating across a page break) because a minimal document could be byte-stable while a realistic one is not. Lives at `apps/workers/scripts/typst-determinism/` with the job in `.github/workflows/verify.yml`. WHAT THIS CLOSES: the risk was that references captured in the arm64 devcontainer could never match x86-64 CI renders, in which case every snapshot test fails on its first run with no useful signal and the remedy is that REFERENCES MUST BE PRODUCED IN CI rather than locally — a change to Day 25's output, not Day 27's. That risk is closed; local capture is sound. STILL NOT COVERED, by design: determinism across Typst VERSIONS (a version bump is expected to change the hash — re-record from arm64, never from the CI side, which would make the check tautological), and determinism of the real templates, which do not exist yet. NEW REQUIREMENT, OPERATOR-SET — THE PIN BELONGS TO THE RENDERER, NOT THE TEST HARNESS. `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` must be set by the production render path itself, not only by tests. The reasoning is that if it is set only in the test harness then production renders are NON-DETERMINISTIC and the snapshot proves a property the real pipeline does not have — the test would be green while the thing it claims to protect is untrue. Concretely, when Day 27 replaces the `render-pdf` consumer: the renderer must pin the timestamp on every invocation, deterministically and from the document's own data rather than from wall-clock time. The obvious candidate is the document's creation timestamp (`generated_documents.created_at`, or the source document's own date), which makes a re-render of the same document reproduce the same bytes — the property snapshot tests and any future document-integrity check actually need. Do NOT leave it to an environment variable that CI happens to set: an env var absent in production is exactly the shape of this defect. Write the chosen source of the timestamp into the ADR that supersedes ADR-013, because it is a correctness property of the renderer and not a test detail. FOLDED IN FROM DAY 25 FOLLOW-UP AND CONFIRMED BY DAY 26: (4) THE STANDING DETERMINISM CHECK MUST RENDER A REAL DOCUMENT, NOT A SYNTHETIC FIXTURE. The `typst-determinism` CI job compiles apps/workers/scripts/typst-determinism/fixture.typ, which has no timestamp in it at all — so it could not have caught the defect Day 26 found, where `generatedAt: new Date()` in the shared loaders made every render of a real document differ from the last. Day 26 proved determinism on all 14 real documents (14/14 byte-identical across two runs), and that is the property the standing check must hold, not a fixture's. When the renderer moves in-process at Day 27, point the check at a real document rendered through the production path and keep the fixture only as a fast smoke test. (5) `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` IS PINNED INSIDE THE RENDER SCRIPT, NOT SUPPLIED BY THE ENVIRONMENT — the production renderer must own it the same way; a CI-supplied env var is not a guarantee that survives a deploy. CLOSED BY DAY 27. (1) The devcontainer xz blocker is fixed at the image: .devcontainer/Dockerfile now installs xz-utils and puts ~/.local/bin on PATH, so `pnpm typst:install` works from the next container rebuild. (2) Provisioning is scripts/install-typst.mjs — pinned version AND a per-architecture sha256, verified before install, with the same version pinned in apps/workers/Dockerfile and .github/workflows/verify.yml; `pnpm typst:check` fails a job whose resolved binary is a different version. The abandoned npm wrapper is not used and there is deliberately no download-on-demand at render time. (3) Cross-arch determinism now runs ON A REAL DOCUMENT: the typst-determinism job seeds a database and renders the 500-serial dispatch note, comparing sha256 against a hash recorded on arm64. The synthetic fixture is deleted — it had no timestamp in it, so it could not have caught the generatedAt defect Day 26 actually found while the fixture sat green. (4) SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH is set by the RENDERER from the document's own instant (src/pdf/typst.ts), not by a harness or an env var, so the snapshots prove a property production actually has. | F.67 | —   | Seed determinism: serial numbers carry a random per-run fragment, so a rendered document cannot be reproduced across a reseed                       | ✅     | 2026-09-12 | Opened by F.38 Day 26 (UNRESOLVED item A in docs/TYPST_DIFF.md, DEV.119). Two parts, both now done, both decided by the operator on the same principle: fix the data, do not weaken the test. PART 1 — SERIALS (DEV.121). packages/db/src/seeds/day13.ts built serial numbers as DSP13-${tenantId.slice(0,4)}-0001 over a defaultRandom() tenant id, so every reseed renamed every serial on every dispatch note. The middle group is now the tenant SLUG: DSP13-demo-0019. Operator: 'A snapshot that skips the serial fragment leaves the product's core data permanently untested.' PART 2 — THE SEED CLOCK (DEV.122). Fixing the serials exposed two larger holes: created_at was defaultNow(), and all 17 data-bearing date call sites across six seed files computed 'N days before today' from Date.now(). packages/db/src/seeds/clock.ts now holds one pinned instant (2026-09-11T17:30:00Z, the moment the Day 25 references were captured, overridable via SEED_EPOCH) and every seed derives from it; packages/db/src/seeds/pin-created-at.ts runs last and derives each row's created_at/updated_at from its own business date, because dispatches are created through the production createDispatchDb helper and threading a test-only override through a protected path to serve a fixture is the wrong trade. Operator: 'Dates appear on every document and are legally relevant, so excluding them leaves a visible field permanently untested.' PROVEN: the database was seeded from scratch twice and all 14 documents rendered after each — 14/14 BYTE-IDENTICAL. Before this, every document differed. COST, accepted deliberately: seeded data no longer ages into the present, so 'last 30 days' views show less as real time passes the epoch. SEED_EPOCH exists for local use; CI and any snapshot run must use the default. NOT COVERED: audit_log rows are written by triggers during the pinning pass and remain wall-clock; nothing renders them onto a document. HANDS TO F.38 SUB-TASK (4): the Day 25 captures survive as the VISUAL sign-off record and as a content contract — 138/138 money figures, 0/14 document numbers and 0/14 face dates differ, and 11/14 documents are character-identical in body text — but they CANNOT be the snapshot baseline. Three body differences remain, none closable by a template: the two DSP-2026-0005 captures carry a serial fragment derived from a tenant uuid that no longer exists, and DSP-REF-0500's page break falls one chip row later (same 500 serials, split 224+276 against 217+283). The footer differs on all 14 by design (document-keyed generatedAt, approved at the Day 26 gate). So Day 27 must RE-CAPTURE the baseline against the pinned seed, from the Chromium pipeline, BEFORE the cutover removes it — recorded in docs/TYPST_DIFF.md with the evidence. ALSO FOUND while answering that question, and fixed here: no Typst template rendered the REV n badge that Header.tsx:62 shows on a quotation with revision > 1. The Day 26 report said '0 UNINTENTIONAL' and was wrong — only one of the 14 cases is a revision, and a visual diff cannot find an element that is absent from one side. Found by character-level text diff; QT-2026-0010's body is now character-identical to its capture. | F.68 | —   | critical-path e2e: an 800ms sleep races the stage-transition commit, and that is the flake's actual cause                                           | ⏳     | —          | Found by flake-triager during F.67 Part 2, while ruling the seed-clock pin OUT as the cause of a flaky run. RULED OUT FIRST, so nobody re-investigates it: the pipeline board is not date-sensitive. apps/web/lib/queries/deals.ts:103 orders by desc(hot), desc(lastActivityAt) — DESCENDING, so a freshly created deal has the maximum last_activity_at and sits toward the TOP of its column; pinning seeded rows into the past moves a new card toward view, not away from it. listDealsByStage has no LIMIT, no OFFSET and no pagination; pipeline-board.tsx:172 maps every card with no virtualiser and droppable-column.tsx clips nothing vertically; and pin-created-at.ts rewrites only created_at/updated_at, which the board does not sort on. The one date filter that exists, deals.ts:73 opts.activeSince, has no caller anywhere in the repo. THE ACTUAL CAUSE: critical-path.spec.ts's moveDealTo does `await page.waitForTimeout(800)` and then `page.goto('/pipeline')`. commitMove fires transitionDealStage inside startTransition, so the navigation aborts the client's read of that response while the server keeps committing. The reloaded page is force-dynamic and server-rendered, so when its SSR query runs before the action's transaction commits, the board renders the card in the OLD column — and the 15s toBeVisible then retries against a static DOM that will never change, burning the full budget. Evidence from the one observed failure: the deal existed in the database at the asserted stage (deal_stage_history shows verbal_commit → po_pending committed at 13:21:37.816Z) while the assertion reported 'element(s) not found', which is the exists-but-not-rendered case rather than a state bug; the failing attempt took 16.9s between those two transitions against 3.6–4.3s in five healthy runs. FIX SHAPE, not yet decided: wait for the server's own signal rather than sleeping — the transition's response, or a visible post-commit change — instead of a fixed 800ms. DO NOT 'fix' this by raising the 15s timeout: the timeout is the symptom and the sleep is the cause, and the standing rule is that no spec gets a longer timeout to hide a race. NOT REPRODUCED in isolation: 5/5 passes standalone with a freshly booted dev server and globalSetup's warm-up. It failed at the END of a full pnpm verify, against a dev server that had already compiled and evicted ~40 routes, which is the condition that makes the race lose. | F.69 | —   | verify.yml runs on PRs into main ONLY, so a stacked PR merges with zero CI — widen the trigger to any branch                                        | ⏳     | —          | Opened by DEV.123; scope settled by DEV.124 after measurement. THE FAULT: .github/workflows/verify.yml triggers on `pull_request: branches: [main]`, so a pull request targeting any other branch runs NO CI at all — not a failure, not a skip, no checks exist. `gh pr checks <n>` reports 'no checks reported', which reads like a queue that has not started rather than a gate that is absent. THE FIX, DECIDED: widen `branches:` so pull requests into any branch run the suite. Do NOT instead add `edited` to `types:`. Widening checks the code BEFORE it enters the intermediate branch, which is where the unchecked merge actually happens; `edited` would only check it after it had been carried upward, and fires on every title and body edit besides. MEASURED, so the cost objection can be weighed rather than assumed: across all 21 pull requests in the repository's history, exactly THREE have ever targeted a non-main base — #16, #17, and #20, the last being a throwaway probe opened to settle this question. So two genuine occurrences in nineteen real PRs. At roughly 9-10 minutes for the e2e job, widening the trigger would have cost about twenty minutes of additional CI across the entire project to date. CONCURRENCY: THE COLLISION DOES NOT EXIST, and the earlier worry that two PRs sharing a head ref could cancel each other was wrong. The group is `${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}`, and on a pull_request event `github.ref` is `refs/pull/<PR number>/merge`, NOT the head branch — confirmed empirically from run 34701098445's log, where actions/checkout runs `git checkout --progress --force refs/remotes/pull/19/merge`. The group is therefore already unique per PR number, so two PRs sharing a head branch land in different groups and neither cancels the other. LEAVE `concurrency` EXACTLY AS IT IS; changing it to key on the PR number would only re-implement what github.ref already provides. The one real consequence of widening is duplicated work rather than cancellation: a head branch with two open PRs (one into main, one into another branch) runs the suite twice per push. Rare, and acceptable. STILL TO CHECK WHEN IMPLEMENTING: the `push: branches: [main]` trigger is deliberately a RECORD and not a gate — main has already begun deploying by the time it runs — so leave it alone; and confirm the ruleset's required status checks still match the job names afterwards, because branch protection matches on job name and a rename silently removes a required check. WHAT THIS TASK DOES NOT COVER: the retargeting half of DEV.123. That is closed by the repository's 'Automatically delete head branches' setting, which was OFF during the trap and is now on — verified by probe PR #20, which retargeted from a deleted base branch to main when PR #19 merged. But #20 arrived at main with ZERO CHECKS, which is precisely why this task survives that setting rather than being closed by it. DO NOT close this by adding a convention asking people not to stack PRs — R22 already carries that, and the point here is the structural half that does not depend on anyone remembering. | F.72 | —   | Dangling DEV/ADR references: correct the citations, never reconstruct the entries                                                                   | ✅     | 2026-09-14 | Found by `verifier` during the Day 27 follow-ups, as the inverse of the duplicate-id problem C6a addresses. THREE IDS WERE CITED THAT HAVE NO ENTRY — DEV.38 in 13 places, DEV.41 in 4, DEV.42 in 1 — and DEVIATIONS.md jumps 37 → 39 → 40 → 43. OPERATOR DIRECTION, and the reason matters: correct the references, do NOT write entries for the missing ids, because composing DEV.38/41/42 now would fabricate a record of decisions nobody made. WHAT WAS RESOLVED. (a) DEV.38 turned out to mean TWO DIFFERENT THINGS in different places, which a blanket replace would have destroyed: in the Typst prompts it meant the page-footer deviation, which is DEV.37 — corrected in docs/F38_TYPST_PLAN.md (3) and docs/DAY_26_PROMPT.md (3), both of which are the operator's own prompts, so the wrong id propagated from a prompt into three documents; in packages/db/src/seeds/day8.ts (2), BUILD_PROMPTS.md and PROJECT_PLAN.md's B.10 row it means a Day 8 seed cross-tenant dealer bug caused by unqualified RLS-bypassed selects, and THAT deviation was never written at all. The day8 comments now describe the bug in place and state that no entry exists. (b) DEV.41 was the prompt's name for the premise that Day 12 deliberately left orders pending; the decision actually taken is recorded as DEV.43, which the citing comment in seeds/day13.ts already referenced — the dangling half is removed. (c) DEV.42 is UNRESOLVABLE: described in the prompt only as 'correlated subquery ambiguity', no entry exists, and nothing in the citing context says what was decided. Recorded as unresolvable rather than guessed. WHAT WAS DELIBERATELY NOT EDITED, each with a reason recorded in scripts/id-reference-allowlist.json: BUILD_PROMPTS.md is a verbatim archive of the prompts as pasted, so editing it would rewrite the record of what was asked; DEVIATIONS.md:410 quotes the original chunk prompt inside DEV.43's 'Spec said' field and is both accurate as a quotation and append-only; docs/TYPST_SPIKE.md and docs/TYPST_DIFF.md name the missing id in order to explain that it is missing. THE PROJECT_PLAN.md CITATION IS STILL WRONG AND IS BLOCKED, which is the one loose end: the B.10 row sits in the hand-maintained Stage B table, and the verifier requires Stage A–E to be byte-identical against main, so correcting it needs either a one-time operator overrule of that rule or F.63, which makes PROJECT_PLAN.md fully generated. F.63 is the better home. THE STANDING FIX: `pnpm check:ids` (scripts/check-id-references.mjs) fails on any cited id without an entry, runs in the CI `checks` job, and is now section 4 of the verifier's remit alongside duplicate detection — C6a catches duplicates on write, this catches dangling on read, and the two together close the id problem from both ends. | F.74 | —   | Sweep for declared-but-unwired values: events in the trackEvent contract that nothing emits, enum values nothing writes                             | ⏳     | —          | Opened by the operator on 2026-09-14 after the pattern cost investigation a second time. THE PATTERN: a value is declared in a contract — an event name, an enum member, a settings key — and nothing ever writes it. It reads as implemented to anyone who greps for it, and is not. This is the placeholder rule the code-auditor agent already states for existence questions ('a declared value with nothing writing it is a placeholder, not an implementation'), but nothing enumerates them, so each is discovered separately at the moment it misleads someone. SCOPE, corrected by `verifier` before this task started: the two instances below are what was KNOWN, not what exists. An enumeration of every trackEvent reference against both event-types.ts files found EIGHT events actually emitted in production — dispatch.created, order.confirmed, quotation.created, quotation.sent, user.logged_in, user.password_changed, email.bounced, email.sent — against 23 declared in each of the two event-types.ts files (mirrors of each other: `diff` reports a single differing line, the header comment on line 13, where each copy names the other as its mirror — the declarations themselves are identical), so FOURTEEN more unemitted events sit behind the two named here (8 emitted + 14 + pdf.generated = 23, which is the arithmetic to check the list against when the sweep runs): tenant.created, dealer.created, product.created, inventory.procurement_created, deal.created, deal.stage_advanced, quotation.accepted, pi.created, pi.confirmed, order.cancelled, payment.recorded, payment.allocated, payment.bounced, dispatch.delivered. Budget for a list of that size. Do NOT go in expecting most of them to classify as DELIBERATE RESERVATION — that was this task’s initial guess and there is evidence against it: Day 17 A3.4 (BUILD_PROMPTS.md:4919-4920) instructed "Wire trackEvent calls at the right points", the first of which is "Inside successful Server Actions, after the DB transaction commits but before returning", a general instruction across the contract rather than a per-event reservation. The split between reservation and gap is the finding, not an input. The two known instances, both found while investigating something else, are: (1) `pdf.generated` is declared in the trackEvent contract on BOTH sides — apps/workers/src/observability/event-types.ts:52 and apps/web/lib/observability/event-types.ts:52, typed { documentId: string; documentType: string } — and emitted nowhere; the only other reference in application code is a web test (apps/web/lib/observability/events.test.ts:67), which asserts the call does not throw; the name also appears in BUILD_PROMPTS.md:4916, in the Day 17 contract that declared it. Found during F.73, where it changed the shape of the fix from 'design telemetry' to 'emit the event the contract already reserves'. (2) The 'invoice' member of the generated_documents document-type enum — declared, and nothing produces it. It has been in the pgEnum since f547dd3 (2026-05-15, "feat(pdf): chunk a — puppeteer worker scaffold + storage schema"), i.e. DAY 10, which is consistent with the Day 10 reservation rationale further down this note. It was described as "from Day 19" in the operator message that opened this task, and that attribution stood in this note until 8e735a8; Day 19 (e3e3afe) is the security day whose audit FOUND the tax invoice missing, not where the enum member was declared. The render-pdf consumer explicitly throws on it (jobs/render-pdf.ts, the not-implemented guard lists quotation, performa_invoice, payment_receipt and dispatch as the implemented set). THE WORK: enumerate, do not fix. Produce a written list of (a) every event name in both event-types.ts files with no emit site, and (b) every enum value in packages/db/src/schema that nothing writes, each marked as either DELIBERATE RESERVATION (the contract is stable ahead of the feature, which is a legitimate pattern — the generated_documents enum was deliberately declared AHEAD OF THE FEATURES in Day 10 so the queue contract would not churn — though note it was not declared COMPLETE: migration 0008 created it with four values (quotation, invoice, dispatch, payment_receipt) and 0010 added performa_invoice the next day (e5ea516, Day 11), so the reservation reduced churn without eliminating it, which is worth weighing before treating "reserved ahead of the feature" as automatically successful) or ACCIDENTAL GAP. The deliverable is the list and the classification; wiring anything is separate work. METHOD NOTE: use affirmative enumeration, not grep-for-absence — read both event-types.ts files and the schema enums in full and check each member against its call sites, rather than grepping for names and trusting empty results. The verdicts are negative-existence claims, which is exactly the shape DEV.115/DEV.118 recorded a silently-failing instrument for. LOW PRIORITY but not zero: it has now cost investigation twice, and the cost falls on whoever is mid-way through something else. ONE REFINEMENT ON THE ENUM INSTANCE, also from `verifier`: 'invoice' is not merely declared — it is accepted UPSTREAM. packages/schemas/src/email.ts:57 validates it and RenderableDocumentType (jobs/render-pdf.ts:36-41) includes it, so a caller can enqueue an invoice render, pass validation, and fail at the guard rather than at the boundary. That is a worse shape than a purely inert declaration and should be classified accordingly. | F.75 | —   | Audit the notes fields flagged by the unearned-precision sweep (counts, exclusivity, negative-existence, sameness claims)                           | ⏳     | —          | Opened by the operator 2026-09-15 after PR #27, where unearned precision in notes fields produced verifier findings round after round. THE SHAPE: a count, an "only", a "first N versions", a "same as", or a version-history claim, asserted in a clause whose sentence carries its real point elsewhere — checkable in one command, and never checked. C6b in docs/BUILD_PROMPT_TEMPLATE.md now bans writing new ones; this task is about the backlog. THE SWEEP, re-runnable rather than merely reported. Every notes field in docs/stage-f-tasks.json, matched case-insensitively against five patterns: (1) /first (version\|two\|three\|four\|five)\\b\|versions of this (note\|task)\|correction pass/; (2) /\\bthe only\\b\|\\bonly (other \|remaining )?reference\\b/; (3) /\\b(nowhere\|never\|nothing (else\|writing\|produces))\\b/; (4) /byte-identical\|byte-for-byte\|identical to/; (5) /\\b(two\|three\|four\|five\|six\|seven\|eight\|nine\|ten\|eleven\|twelve\|thirteen\|fourteen\|twenty-three\|\\d{1,3})\\s+(sites?\|citations?\|places?\|files?\|calls?\|events?\|versions?\|occurrences?\|declarations?\|references?\|captures?\|attempts?\|tests?)\\b/. Counting every match of every pattern gave 83 across the 50 notes-bearing tasks of 75, at bc6342f. The figure moves with the fifth pattern's word list, so re-run rather than trust it. WHERE THE SUBSTANCE IS: pattern 3 supplies 40 of the 83, 31 of them a bare `never`, and about two thirds of those assert a CHECKABLE ABSENCE — "Advisory was never reachable" (F.2a), "2 verify-day-c2 tests never ran" (F.52), "asserts a fix that was never made" (F.58). The rest are rules, state labels or a conditional, not claims at all. So pattern 3 is both the noisiest by volume and the most productive by content, and needs the most reading per match. It is also the least EVIDENCED of the five: no PR #27 finding was purely of that shape. DO NOT AUDIT THIS NOW — operator instruction, and the reason is the point: "auditing 50 tasks of historical notes has no reader and would generate its own claims." If it is ever picked up, audit only PENDING and IN_PROGRESS notes, where a wrong claim can still mislead someone into building the wrong thing. A wrong count in a completed task's notes has no consequence. This backlog may correctly stay unaudited forever. | F.76 | —   | Fix the self-falsifying "byte-for-byte mirror" header comment in both event-types.ts files                                                          | ⏳     | —          | Found 2026-09-14 during PR #27 and deliberately not folded in, per CLAUDE.md §10.1. THE DEFECT: apps/workers/src/observability/event-types.ts:13 and apps/web/lib/observability/event-types.ts:13 each read "A byte-for-byte mirror lives in <the other path>". That line is the ONLY difference between the two files — `diff` reports 13c13 and nothing else — so the comment is falsified by its own existence. WHY IT IS WORTH A TASK rather than a drive-by fix: the wrong claim propagated. It was copied out of the header into F.74's notes as "two byte-identical event-types.ts files", which was caught on PR #27 only by a character-level check of the two files, after being read for plausibility and passing. A comment asserting a property the file does not have is a source someone else will quote. THE FIX is a wording change only, no code: say that the two files mirror each other except for this line (e.g. "This file is mirrored at <path>; the two are identical apart from this comment"), in both copies. Do NOT attempt to make the files actually byte-identical — the header naming the other path is useful, and a shared module is a real refactor with an import-boundary question (web and workers are separate builds) that does not belong in a comment fix. NOTE FOR WHOEVER DOES IT: verify with `diff` after editing, not by eye, and if the two files then differ on more than the comment line, that is a finding. | F.77 | —   | Decide what to do about the two ## DEV.64 headings (an entry and its closure note sharing one id)                                                   | ⏳     | —          | Pre-existing on main; `verifier` reports it every run and correctly declines to charge it to any branch. WHAT IT ACTUALLY IS, from reading both entries rather than the duplicate-heading grep: not two deviations colliding on one id. DEVIATIONS.md:994 is "DEV.64 — Stage C — repo `.do/app.yaml` is documentation, not the deployed spec" (2026-05-22) and :1582 is "DEV.64 — closure note — operator-driven spec sync (Stage D Day D.2)" (closed 2026-05-29), whose body opens "Original DEV.64 (Stage C) documented that…". The second is the RESOLVED entry for the first, written the way C6 prescribes but given the same heading. So every citation resolves to one subject and no reader is misled; what breaks is tooling that keys on heading uniqueness. This reading was already on record in docs/BUILD_PROMPT_TEMPLATE.md and .claude/agents/verifier.md, which both call it a resolution that reused the id. THE CONSTRAINT: both headings are historic and on main, and DEVIATIONS.md is append-only, so NEITHER can be renamed in place. THREE OPTIONS, recommendation (c): (a) append an entry explaining that the two are one deviation plus its closure — costs a third DEV.64 mention to explain the first two; (b) a one-time operator overrule of append-only — DEV.112 establishes that is not the main thread's call, and it is disproportionate to a cosmetic duplicate; (c) LEAVE THE FILE ALONE and teach the checker that a heading marked as a closure note for an existing id is a legitimate second occurrence, then record the decision so a reader of a verifier report knows the DEV.64 line is expected. IF (c) IS TAKEN, three sites need the "expected, do not report" disposition — C6a's worked example in docs/BUILD_PROMPT_TEMPLATE.md (the "Do not derive the next id by eye" paragraph), the Deviations-log restatement in the same file, and the duplicate-id section of .claude/agents/verifier.md. Locate them by grepping DEV.64 across docs/ and .claude/. C6a's example is the one that is actually MIS-FRAMED: it cites this as an id derived by eye from an unsorted file, which the other two sites contradict. Confirm that reading independently before amending it — the alternative, that the id really was picked by eye and the closure framing came later, is not excluded by either entry. | F.78 | —   | Six latent renderer-hardening items left by F.63 (ranked, none breaks a delivered guarantee)                                                        | ⏳     | —          | Filed 2026-09-15 on operator instruction — "a commit message is not a backlog". These are the items the F.63 closeout review ranked as NOT blocking a merge, in its order. All are reachable only through content nobody writes by accident, all are idempotent and leave `plan:check` green, and none breaks a guarantee F.63 claims. (1) `## Stage F Changelog` and `## Changelogs` render through. The banned name is anchored immediately after the hashes and terminated with `\\b`, so a heading that merely CONTAINS it is not matched. Whether either is the section DEV.110 banned is genuinely arguable — decide that before widening, because widening catches legitimate headings too. (2) A `subPhase` that sanitizes to empty renders `### (Day 1)`. Cosmetic; the alternative is rejecting the task, which is worse for a value that is only ever a grouping label. (3) Two sub-phases differing only by a control character collapse into two identically-titled sections. Cosmetic and self-inflicted only. (4) `days: '-5'` renders `(Days 0–5)` because the day parser takes the minimum of the parsed numbers and a leading minus is dropped by the split. Validating `days` as a number or range would fix it and would also reject the legitimate `—` placeholder, so it needs a shape decision first. (5) The `docs/PROJECT_HISTORY.md` Changelog assertion now shares the renderer's matchers, which closes the gap the review found — listed here only so the ranking is complete. NOTHING HERE IS URGENT. The reason to keep the list is that four of the six defects the review DID find were of exactly this shape and were dismissed as unreachable until someone reached them. (6) ADDED 2026-09-16, AND UNLIKE THE OTHER FIVE THIS ONE ALREADY REACHED main-BOUND OUTPUT. THE MECHANISM, stated in both directions because the first version of this item got it half right and was corrupted by the half it omitted: a bare underscore or a bare asterisk sitting at a WORD BOUNDARY in a task notes field can pair with another one elsewhere in the SAME rendered table cell, and the renderer emits the pair as Markdown emphasis — asterisks come out as underscores and UNDERSCORES COME OUT AS ASTERISKS. INTRAWORD underscores are safe, which is why the PILOT filename constants render correctly and a trailing-underscore glob does not; the hazard is delimiter POSITION, not the character. THE TRANSFORM IS PRETTIER, called in formatBlock() at scripts/sync-project-plan.ts, and it runs AFTER sanitize() — which is why a per-input guard cannot see it and why the fix belongs on the output. LIVE INSTANCES, BOTH DIRECTIONS. Asterisk direction: F.37's notes briefly carried a glob for the PNGs under docs/client-evidence/, it paired with the PILOT glob, PROJECT_PLAN.md acquired a citation to a file that does not exist, pnpm check:paths named the file and the line, and CI went red. Underscore direction: the FIRST VERSION OF THIS VERY ITEM wrote the PILOT glob twice with its trailing underscore, and both rendered as an asterisk in PROJECT_PLAN.md — new on that branch, absent from main, found by the closeout verifier reading the rendered output rather than the source. WHAT MAKES IT WORSE THAN THE OTHER FIVE: it is INVISIBLE UNTIL A SECOND DELIMITER EXISTS. The asterisk-direction text rendered escaped and inert one commit earlier and passed every gate; it became a dangling citation only when an unrelated edit landed BETWEEN the two delimiters and changed how they paired. A notes field that renders correctly today can be corrupted by an edit somewhere else in the same cell, with nothing in either edit looking wrong. MEASURED EXPOSURE, so the fix is not scoped by guesswork: of the underscore-bearing tokens in this file, exactly one DISTINCT token does not survive into the rendered plan, and it is the trailing-underscore PILOT glob in F.37's notes — inherited, and live on main. Item 6's first version added two further instances of that same token and those are gone, so what remains is the pre-existing one, which is also the one the asterisk-direction failure paired with. Re-run it boundary-aware — a substring test reports a trailing-underscore token as present because it is a prefix of a longer identifier, so the naive version of this check is vacuous and says zero. STILL LIVE ON main: the PILOT glob renders mangled in PROJECT_PLAN.md today, identically before and after the merge that surfaced this, verified by rendering both. It is cosmetic there only because that string is not a docs/ path, which is the sole reason check:paths does not see it. THE FIX SHAPE: escape or collapse BOTH delimiters at word boundaries in the cell and heading paths the way control characters already are, and assert it on the OUTPUT in assertRenderedOk() rather than per input field — the approach the F.63 review adopted after six defects in three rounds all turned out to be a guard on one input path with the next route in through a different character. This item is the seventh of exactly that shape, and the character it came in through was the one the previous fix did not name. Recorded in DEV.132 section 6 and DEV.134. | F.79 | —   | Stage 0-E content in docs/PROJECT_HISTORY.md has no guarantee against silent rewriting — decide whether to replace the one F.63 removed             | ⏳     | —          | Filed 2026-09-15 on operator instruction, and deliberately left OPEN rather than closed: "Per-section floors and mutation testing are a different guarantee, not the same one. Keep it visible rather than closed." Recorded in DEV.131. WHAT WAS REMOVED: before F.63, the closeout rule was "no change outside the STAGE_F_TASKS markers, full stop", and its substantive effect was that Stage 0 and Stages A-E COULD NOT BE SILENTLY REWRITTEN — any edit to them failed the gate. WHAT REPLACED IT: nothing in kind. `docs/PROJECT_HISTORY.md` is hand-maintained, has no sync step, no deny rule in `.claude/settings.json`, no append-only requirement, and `.claude/agents/verifier.md` explicitly tells the verifier NOT to report edits to it as containment failures. What exists instead is ordinary review plus assertions in `scripts/sync-project-plan.test.ts`: the six stage headings survive, every table-bearing section holds at or above its migrated row count, every Stage B day row stays populated, no malformed rows, and the pilot tenant and Stage-E-did-not-complete records survive. Those catch DELETION and EMPTYING. They do not catch a changed date, a changed status symbol, a rewritten note, or a swapped row — which is what the old rule did catch. WHY THE TRADE WAS STILL RIGHT: the old guarantee was unsatisfiable, not strict — it also forbade every legitimate edit, which is what forced DEV.112's overrule and what F.63 existed to dissolve. Trading an unsatisfiable guarantee for a partial one is a real improvement and a real loss at the same time, and the loss is the half that tends to go unrecorded. THE PROPOSED FIX, adopted as this task's direction by the operator 2026-09-16 rather than left as an open menu: CHECKSUM STAGE 0 THROUGH STAGE D AND LEAVE STAGE E EDITABLE. WHY IT IS BETTER THAN WHAT WAS LOST, which is the operator's reasoning and the part worth keeping: the old rule was a BLANKET DENY on a whole file, which is why it also forbade every legitimate edit and had to be overruled once (DEV.112). A targeted integrity check does the opposite — it asserts immutability only over content that SHOULD be immutable, and leaves Stage E open precisely because Stage E is not finished and its rows will legitimately change when the pilot resumes. So this is not a restoration of the old guarantee; it is a narrower and more accurate one. SHAPE, for whoever implements it: a committed manifest of per-section digests for Stage 0, A, B, C and D; a check that recomputes them and fails on drift, run beside check:ids and check:paths; and a documented way to re-baseline a section deliberately, since a legitimate correction to closed history must be possible or this becomes the same unsatisfiable rule in a smaller box. Stage E, the deferred-feature list, the critical path and the risk register are all excluded — they are live. THE OTHER OPTIONS, recorded so the choice is legible: (a) accept it, which is how every other document in the repo is protected; (b) make the whole file append-only like DEVIATIONS.md, wrong for a file whose Stage E rows must change; (d) generate the closed sections, which reintroduces exactly what F.63 removed. DO NOT CLOSE THIS TASK ON THE GROUNDS THAT THE FLOOR TESTS AND MUTATION TESTING EXIST — operator instruction, restated here because a later cleanup pass is exactly where that would happen. Those catch deletion and emptying. A floor notices six rows becoming zero; it does not notice six rows becoming six different rows. DO NOT CLOSE THIS BY POINTING AT THE FLOOR TESTS. They are a different guarantee, and conflating the two is how the loss stops being visible. | F.80 | —   | Decide the home for the client evidence — docs/CLIENT_CONTEXT.md or docs/STAGE_F_BUILD_v3.md §7 — and make the other a pointer                      | ✅     | 2026-09-16 | Filed 2026-09-16 rather than done, per CLAUDE.md §11.2 — the task that created the duplication is not the one that should resolve it. WHAT EXISTS NOW: docs/CLIENT_CONTEXT.md consolidates the client facts that were previously addressable only inside docs/STAGE_F_BUILD_v3.md — the MA/26-27/1079 voucher arithmetic and the Rs 557.02 collapsed-ledger finding (§7), the screenshot-to-filename mapping (§7), the turnover table and the Rs 5 crore e-invoicing threshold that put e-invoice in go-live scope (§0), the e-way bill 180-day window (§6), the four open client asks and the two open serial-scan decisions (§7). Its header states that docs/STAGE_F_BUILD_v3.md is the origin and wins on any disagreement. THE PROBLEM THAT CREATES: two copies of the same evidence. The v3 header calls a hand-maintained second copy of a shared record "the exact drift that produced a stale SECURITY_AUDIT.md and a wrong Day 19 plan". The origin-wins line bounds the damage; it does not remove the copy, and a reader who finds only one of the two files has no way to know the other exists unless the pointer is in the file they found. THE OPTIONS: (a) CLIENT_CONTEXT becomes the home and §7 is cut to a pointer — cleanest, but §7 is cited by path from other documents and the cut must land with pnpm check:paths green; (b) §7 stays the home and CLIENT_CONTEXT is deleted — which gives up the addressable client-facing document that motivated it, and F.37's notes already record that STAGE_F_BUILD_v3.md stays durable precisely because it is "the only home for the client evidence"; (c) keep both, and record why the duplication is accepted and who re-syncs it. NO RECOMMENDATION IS MADE HERE. SEQUENCING: settle this BEFORE F.37 moves either file, so the move happens once rather than twice. RESOLVED 2026-09-16 BY OPERATOR RULING, AND IT IS NONE OF THE THREE OPTIONS ABOVE: both files stay, with a stated relationship. docs/STAGE_F_BUILD_v3.md section 7 is the EVIDENCE RECORD — provenance and reasoning, written once, rarely changed. docs/CLIENT_CONTEXT.md is the WORKING REFERENCE a session reads before a client-facing task, and it changes as asks close and decisions land. THE ANTI-DRIFT RULE, which is what makes two files safe: CLIENT_CONTEXT cites section 7 as its source and DUPLICATES NO REASONING — facts and pointers only. If the two disagree, SECTION 7 WINS AND THE COPY IS THE BUG; fix it in CLIENT_CONTEXT, not in section 7. The operator's reason for needing the rule rather than trusting the convention: section 7's own screenshot renumbering already shows the live risk, where every citation resolved to the wrong image and each wrong one looked exactly as authoritative as a right one. BUILT: the rule is recorded in BOTH files — as the header block of docs/CLIENT_CONTEXT.md and as a block immediately under the section 7 heading in docs/STAGE_F_BUILD_v3.md — so a reader who finds either one learns the relationship. docs/CLIENT_CONTEXT.md was rewritten to comply: multi-sentence rationale was replaced by a one-line fact plus a section pointer throughout, while every number, name, date, decision and open question was kept. What counts as "reasoning" in that trim was a judgement call and is recorded in DEV.133. Because the loaders live in the same files, the files still import renderToStaticMarkup, so react and react-dom remain dependencies of a workers process that renders no HTML. THE WORK: move each loader into its own .ts module, delete the React render halves and \_components/, drop react/react-dom from apps/workers/package.json. WHY IT IS SEPARATE: it touches every document path's data loading, which is the one part of the pipeline the cutover deliberately left untouched so that a Phase 2 difference could only be attributable to rendering. Doing both at once would have made any diff ambiguous. CHECK WHEN DOING IT: styles.ts is still the transcription source for \_lib/chrome.typ's px() values and palette — the Typst templates were built from it, so deleting it loses the provenance of every size and colour unless that is recorded first. | F.71 | —     | Two production values are now oversized by orders of magnitude after the Typst cutover — worker instance size and PDF_RENDER_TIMEOUT_MS | ⏳     | —          | Opened by F.38 Day 27 with the evidence attached, and deliberately NOT applied that day. Both values were sized for Chromium and both are now far larger than the work they cover. MEASURED AFTER THE CUTOVER, on the heaviest document in the corpus (the 500-serial dispatch note), ten consecutive renders: peak RSS 119.6 MB against a 108.5 MB baseline — an 11 MB working set — and render wall time 57-125ms, median 66ms. (1) WORKER INSTANCE SIZE. Production runs basic-xs (1 GB), raised off basic-xxs (512 MB) after the worker OOM-restarted under Chromium rendering (DEV.67). The memory profile that caused that OOM no longer exists: there is no browser process, no binary extraction, no page cache. 512 MB would now carry roughly 4x headroom over the measured peak. (2) PDF_RENDER_TIMEOUT_MS is 120000. It was sized for a 60-90s COLD CHROMIUM LAUNCH (DEV.66/DEV.67) plus margin. Against a 66ms median it is roughly 1,800x the work. Note the asymmetry before tightening it: a generous timeout costs only how long a genuinely stuck render takes to surface, while a tight one turns a slow render into a user-visible failure — 10000 would still be ~150x the median. WHY THIS IS NOT APPLIED YET: both are LIVE-SPEC values (DEV.64 — the repo's .do/\*.yaml are documentation; the deployed spec is authoritative), so changing them is an operator action against production, not a commit. The evidence is recorded in .do/app.production.yaml as comments beside each value so it is found by whoever changes them. SEQUENCE WITH F.35, which downsizes the production worker instance, the web DB pools and the Postgres tier as one coupled package: the worker instance size in this task IS one of F.35's three parameters, so do not move it independently or the two tasks will fight. F.35's own note warns the three must move together or the pool caps overrun the tier connection budget, and F.35's cost premise has already been corrected once — so re-derive rather than trusting the recorded numbers. PDF_RENDER_TIMEOUT_MS is NOT part of F.35's coupled package and can move on its own. Record the exact prior values in docs/PRODUCTION_ENV.md before changing anything, per F.35; F.42 restores them.
